title: Irregular Periods: What's Typical and What Warrants a Visit
content:
Menstrual cycles vary naturally from person to person, and even from month to month in the same person, so a certain amount of irregularity is expected rather than automatically abnormal. That said, there are specific patterns that are worth bringing to a clinician's attention rather than waiting out.

A useful starting point is comparing a cycle to a person's own typical pattern rather than to a generic "28 days." A sudden, sustained change — cycles that were once predictable and are now consistently much shorter, much longer, or unpredictable — is more meaningful than a single unusual month.

Specific patterns that are generally considered worth discussing with a healthcare provider include: periods that stop for more than about three months (90 days) when pregnancy has been ruled out; periods that become irregular after having been regular for some time; bleeding so heavy that it soaks through a pad or tampon every hour or less for two or more consecutive hours; bleeding that lasts longer than about ten days regardless of how heavy it is; and new symptoms alongside cycle changes, such as unexplained night sweats, hot flashes, or significant pelvic pain.

Many different, often unrelated, things can cause irregular periods, which is part of why a clinician's evaluation is useful rather than trying to self-diagnose. Common contributors include pregnancy or the postpartum/breastfeeding period; significant weight changes or disordered eating; high levels of physical or emotional stress; thyroid conditions (both underactive and overactive thyroid can disrupt cycles); polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and other hormonal conditions; uterine fibroids or polyps; and changes in the uterine lining itself, such as endometrial hyperplasia. Certain medications, including some contraceptives and treatments that affect hormone levels, can also change bleeding patterns as an expected side effect.

Age and life stage matter too. It's common for cycles to be irregular in the first one to two years after periods start, as the hormonal feedback loop that governs ovulation is still maturing. Irregularity is also extremely common in the years leading up to menopause (perimenopause), as hormone production becomes less predictable before stopping altogether.

When a clinician evaluates irregular periods, they typically start with a detailed history — including cycle length and heaviness over time, other symptoms, medications, weight changes, and stress — followed by a physical exam and, depending on the picture, blood tests (such as thyroid function or hormone levels) or imaging like a pelvic ultrasound. There is rarely a single test that immediately explains irregular cycles; it's usually a process of narrowing down possibilities.

Tracking cycle length, flow heaviness, and associated symptoms for a few months before an appointment can make this evaluation much more efficient, since it gives the clinician real data rather than a general impression. None of this is a substitute for that evaluation — this is general information intended to help someone recognize when a pattern is worth raising, not to diagnose the cause on its own.
